stem: Which of the following is FALSE in regards to medication use in pregnancy?

options.html: With few exceptions, poor control of disease tends to have greater impact on pregnancy outcome than drug therapies
Clearance of most drugs is increased in pregnancy
Conversations surrounding the teratogenicity of drugs should occur at ~8 weeks gestation, before organogenesis begins
Effective drugs that have been used for longer periods of time are preferable to newer drugs
Use of drugs in pregnancy should be minimized to only those that are necessary and for the shortest period of time possible

answer: The correct answer is C. Two things are wrong with it. Conversations about teratogenicity should occur at the time of prescription in any woman of childbearing age — not once she is already pregnant. And the majority of organogenesis has already occurred by 8 weeks, so 8 weeks is not "before organogenesis begins".

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q85-Q87. Tests [[03 - Teratogenesis]], [[10 - Drugs Used in Gynecology]].
stem: Maria is a 24 y.o. woman with a history of depression who comes to you with a positive pregnancy test. Her depression has been well controlled on Fluoxetine, an SSRI antidepressant, for the past 6 years. She worries about the effect of this medication - what should you do?

options.html: Antidepressants are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy, stop the drug immediately and refer to a psychologist for counseling in order to control her depression during her pregnancy
Fluoxetine is associated with malformations, therefore you should start her on a newer antidepressant which has not yet been shown to be associated with birth defects
In order to avoid withdrawal of both Maria and the fetus from the antidepressant, you should wean her off the drug slowly and remain drug-free for the duration of the pregnancy
Start another agent such as valproic acid in order achieve optimum control of her depression and prevent any deterioration during her pregnancy
Stay on the same dose of fluoxetine to maintain control of her depression

answer:
The correct answer is E. Depression in pregnancy is itself associated with bad outcomes, so maintaining treatment matters. Fluoxetine has been studied, and malformations arise at the same rate in fluoxetine-exposed women as in the general population.

B inverts the correct principle (see Q85D): it is better to use effective drugs with a long track record than newer alternatives that have not been studied as extensively. D is actively dangerous — valproic acid is known to cause neural tube defects and should not be added to a pregnant woman's regimen unless completely necessary.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q85-Q87. Tests [[03 - Teratogenesis]], [[10 - Drugs Used in Gynecology]].
stem: Which of the following drugs is NOT a known teratogen?
answer: The correct answer is D. Acetaminophen is the safe one; warfarin, lithium, misoprostol and ethanol are all known teratogens.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: Which of the following soft markers of aneuploidy is most strongly associated with fetal morbidity?
answer:
The correct answer is A. A thickened nuchal fold is associated with Down syndrome and carries an odds ratio of 20-25x.

Do not confuse the two nuchal measurements: nuchal fold thickness is measured on the second-trimester scan (~18-22 weeks); nuchal translucency is measured in the first trimester (see Q104).

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: An increased nuchal translucency may suggest:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Nuchal translucency is a component of integrated prenatal screening and an effective screening tool for chromosomal abnormalities and congenital malformations. Increased NT can also be present in a normal pregnancy.

D is the exception to note: although IPS overall has a high detection rate for neural tube defects, NT measurement alone is not effective in detecting NTDs. See prenatal screening.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: Which of the following tests is useful for prenatal diagnosis:
answer:
The correct answer is E. The question hinges on diagnosis vs. screening:

  • DIAGNOSTIC: amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, ultrasound
  • SCREENING: IPS, nuchal translucency, soft markers, serum screening

Only E is a diagnostic test. See prenatal screening.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90, Q104-Q106. Tests [[02 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada]].
stem: Which of the following patients should be offered prenatal diagnosis by invasive testing?

options.html: 24-year-old G1P0 with a previous history of one early pregnancy loss
29-year-old G3P2 with a family history of T2DM
19-year-old primigravida woman with a normal prenatal screen
31-year-old G2P1 whose partner is a balanced translocation carrier

answer:
The correct answer is E. Indications for prenatal diagnosis by invasive testing:

  • Advanced maternal age (>37 years) — note that makes A, at 35, insufficient
  • Previous child with a chromosome abnormality
  • A parent is a balanced translocation carrier
  • Family history of a genetic disorder diagnosable prenatally
  • Positive findings on prenatal screen or ultrasound

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What is the most commonly known cause of spontaneous abortion?
answer: The correct answer is D. Approximately 15-20% of all clinical pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion. In most cases the cause is unknown — but when the cause is known, the most common contributor is an inherent abnormality of the fetus. Note the careful wording of the question: "most commonly known cause".

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What is the normal doubling time of hCG in a healthy early pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is D. Normal doubling time in early pregnancy (<10 weeks) is about 48-72 hours. If hCG rises less than 85% over 48 hours, there is a greater association with abnormal pregnancy.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What is the most common cause of ectopic pregnancy?

options.html: Use of an intra-uterine contraceptive device (IUD)

answer:
The correct answer is B. PID — including puerperal and post-abortal sepsis — is the #1 cause of ectopic pregnancy.

A is the classic trap: a pregnancy in an IUD user is more likely to be ectopic, because the device protects against an intrauterine pregnancy specifically. But pregnancy in an IUD user is rare, so the IUD is not a common cause of ectopics.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q91-Q94. Tests [[07 - Approach to First Trimester Bleeding & Ultrasound]], [[08 - Pathology of 1st Trimester Bleeding]].
stem: What diagnosis is suggested by the following pathological findings: large hydropic villi involving all tissue, trophoblast proliferation?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A complete molar pregnancy occurs when both chromosome sets are of paternal origin. Diagnosis is made clinically but confirmed histologically.

Complete molePartial mole
Fetusabsentabnormal fetus may be present
Villilarge, swollen, hydropic — ALL tissuesmaller hydropic villi interspersed with normal villi
Trophoblast proliferationmarkedless

See gestational trophoblastic disease.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Routine morphology is performed via ultrasound at 18-20 weeks gestation. What is the prevalence of major anomalies found in the general population?
answer: The correct answer is B. 2-3%.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a common symptom/complaint in a pregnant woman at 34 weeks gestation?
answer: The correct answer is C. Nausea and vomiting are much more common in the first trimester and are usually not present in the third. All the other listed complaints are common in the third trimester.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q89, Q95, Q98. Tests [[04 - Topics of Antenatal Care]], [[09 - Second Trimester Ultrasound]].
stem: Which of the following fetal assessment tools is the most predictive of perinatal mortality?
answer:
The correct answer is B. FMC, NST and BPP all provide helpful information but really only give a "snapshot" of what is happening with the fetus, and have no effect on perinatal mortality rate.

Umbilical artery Doppler, by contrast, is predictive of morbidity and mortality — and if normal, is associated with a decreased PMR.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: A 28-year-old primigravida presents to the obstetrics clinic at 24 weeks gestation with complaints of headache and blurred vision. On examination, her blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg and her urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria. Which of the following is a likely consequence of the abnormality of uterine spiral arteries seen in this patient?

options.html: Increased risk of fetal growth restriction
Increased risk of preterm premature rupture of membranes

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is pre-eclampsia — hypertension plus proteinuria developing after 20 weeks. One of the underlying mechanisms is thought to be abnormal remodeling of the uterine spiral arteries, which leads to inadequate blood flow to the placenta and therefore impaired fetal growth.

Fetal growth restriction is a common complication of pre-eclampsia and can cause significant morbidity and mortality if not managed, which is why close monitoring matters. Note that A and B are both the wrong direction — pre-eclampsia increases the risk of preterm labour and abruption.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: Which of the following describes normal variations in blood pressure throughout pregnancy?

options.html: BP falls to lowest point in T1, increases slightly in T2 and rises to highest level in T3
BP remains normal during T1, falls in T2, and returns to normal at term
BP remains normal during T1, falls in T2, and increases to hypertension in T3
BP increases in T1, remains high in T2, and falls to lowest levels near term
Blood pressure should remain steady during pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is B. Blood pressure normally drops in the second trimester, because pregnant women are relatively vasodilated — but BP should return to normal at term. Option C is the trap: a rise to hypertension in T3 is pathological (pre-eclampsia), not a normal variation.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman presents at 34 weeks after a normal course of pregnancy. She is now presenting with weight gain of 6 lb. in the past 2 weeks. Her BP is 148/100, and her urine contains 2+ protein. The best management of this woman is:

options.html: Ensure fetal well-being, rule out adverse conditions and deliver at term
Induction of labour regardless of gestational age
Monitor fetal well-being and, and administer MgSO4 and antihypertensives

answer:
The correct answer is C. This woman has mild pre-eclampsia (BP >140/90, proteinuria >1+). Management: identify the underlying cause, rule out adverse conditions, ensure fetal wellbeing, increase maternal/fetal surveillance, and deliver at term if investigations are normal.

D and E are the severe pre-eclampsia answers: delivery regardless of gestational age, plus antihypertensives and MgSO4. Compare directly with Q102, where the numbers are severe.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents with a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg and 4+ proteinuria. Which of the following is NOT a recommended initial management option for this patient?

options.html: Administration of magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
Initiation of antihypertensive therapy to lower blood pressure
Delivery of the fetus and placenta as soon as possible
Hospitalization for close monitoring and management

answer:
The correct answer is C. This patient has severe pre-eclampsia — defined as BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg with 4+ proteinuria. Initial management is MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis, antihypertensives if needed, and hospitalization for close monitoring.

Delivery is the definitive treatment, but not an initial management option — the timing must be weighed against gestational age and disease severity. In general, delivery is recommended after 34 weeks; earlier only if needed to prevent maternal or fetal complications. At 33 weeks, "as soon as possible" is premature.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Workbook Q77, Q100-Q103. Tests [[11 - Hypertension in Pregnancy]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a risk factor for the development of preeclampsia?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Risk factors for pre-eclampsia: age <20 or >35, BMI >35, hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, connective tissue disease, previous pre-eclampsia, first pregnancies or pregnancies after an interval of >10 years, and multiple gestations.

Age 33 falls inside the safe window (neither <20 nor >35) — that's the whole point of the option. Note BMI 36 clears the >35 threshold.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q80, Q121. Tests [[01 - Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation]].
stem: Which of the following placental abnormalities may occur from the placenta being implanted too shallowly in the uterus?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Sort the options by what went wrong with implantation:

  • Too deeply → accreta, increta, percreta
  • Wrong location (obstructing the cervical os) → previa
  • Too shallowly → abruption, because a shallowly implanted placenta is more likely to detach from the uterine wall — which can cause hemorrhage, shock, and both fetal and maternal death.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q80, Q121. Tests [[01 - Antepartum Hemorrhage & Abnormal Placentation]].
stem: Fetal cells present in the maternal circulation on a Kleihauer Betke test suggests
answer: The correct answer is C. Placental abruption.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The logic: the Kleihauer-Betke test detects fetal red cells that have crossed into maternal blood, which requires a breach of the fetomaternal interface — i.e. the placenta shearing away from the uterine wall.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q96-Q97. Tests [[02 - Approach to the Small Fetus]].
stem: Which of the following is NOT a common fetal risk in post-term pregnancy?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Post-term pregnancy is defined as pregnancy extending beyond 42 weeks. Risks include macrosomia, birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, prolonged labour, operative delivery), post-maturity syndrome and death.

The direction is the discriminator: post-term pregnancy causes oligohydramnios, not polyhydramnios — which can in turn cause complications such as intolerance of labour.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q96-Q97. Tests [[02 - Approach to the Small Fetus]].
stem: An ultrasound is performed to assess fetal growth and reports an asymmetric intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). The most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Split IUGR by symmetry:

  • Asymmetric — 70-80% of cases; caused by uteroplacental insufficiency (abruption, circumvallate placenta, etc.)
  • Symmetric — 20-30% of cases; most often caused by an early severe insult such as infection or chromosomal abnormality

The logic: a late insult spares the already-grown head (asymmetric); an early insult stunts everything at once (symmetric).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for premature labour?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A previous premature delivery is the strongest risk factor for premature labour:

  • 15% risk with 1 previous preterm birth
  • 30% risk with 2 previous preterm births

Other important risk factors: PROM, indications for preterm induction including pre-eclampsia, multiple gestation and placental abnormalities. But 50% of all preterm deliveries have no identifiable cause.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: A 32 year-old primigravida woman presents to the emergency department with premature rupture of membranes at 37 weeks gestation. She does not have a fever and has not yet experienced any contractions. Appropriate management at this time is:

options.html: Tocolysis for 48-72 hours to allow for transfer to birth unit
Observation for spontaneous onset of labour
Immediate induction of labour and administration of MgSO4 and antenatal steroids
Urgent Caesarean section followed by administration of antibiotics
Insertion of an intrauterine pressure monitor

answer:
The correct answer is B. At 37 weeks this is TERM PROM without labour — the gestational age is the whole question. Management of term PROM: allow spontaneous labour, induce with oxytocin at ~6 h if labour does not begin naturally, and GBS prophylaxis.

Contrast the two things the distractors describe:

  • Preterm PROM → antibiotic therapy, antenatal steroids, induction at ~36 weeks
  • Preterm labour → tocolysis × 48 h, antenatal betamethasone, GBS prophylaxis

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q108-Q110. Tests [[03 - Approach to Preterm Labor]].
stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for preterm labour?
answer:
The correct answer is D. First pregnancy is not a risk factor for preterm labour.

Note that this cuts against the intuition built in Q103, where first pregnancy is a risk factor — for pre-eclampsia. Different outcome, different risk profile.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The cardinal movements of normal labour in CORRECT ORDER are:

options.html: Engagement, Flexion, Descent, Extension, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Expulsion
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal Rotation, Extension, External Rotation, Expulsion.
Descent, Engagement, Flexion, Extension, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Expulsion.
Descent, Engagement, Internal Rotation, Flexion, External Rotation, Extension, Expulsion.
Engagement, Descent, Flexion, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Flexion, Extension, Expulsion.

answer: The correct answer is B. Engagement → Descent → Flexion → Internal Rotation → Extension → External Rotation → Expulsion.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The discriminators across the options: engagement precedes descent (eliminates C and D), flexion precedes internal rotation (eliminates A and D), and extension precedes external rotation (eliminates E, which also lists flexion twice).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the initiation of labour?

options.html: High levels of progesterone at term

answer:
The correct answer is D. Progesterone is high throughout pregnancy, but is decreased relative to estrogen at term. It is therefore progesterone withdrawal that initiates labour — not high progesterone levels.

The genuine contributors: oxytocin, prostaglandin, withdrawal of relaxin and prostacyclin, and fetal triggers such as HPA axis activation.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The second stage of labour is defined as:

options.html: Onset of labour to full dilatation
Cervical dilation of 5 cm with regular uterine contractions
Full dilation to delivery of fetus
Autotransfusion and hemodynamic shift occurring after birth

answer: The correct answer is C. Second stage = full dilation → delivery of the fetus.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. For the full set: first stage = onset of labour → full dilatation (option A); third stage = delivery of the fetus → expulsion of the placenta (see Q115).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The target nerves for pain control during the first stage of labour are:
answer: The correct answer is B. First-stage pain is best controlled by targeting T10-T12. This pain is often experienced as back pain, which is the clue to its level. Options for pain control in labour: epidural, pudendal block, general anesthetic, Lamaze breathing.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q111-Q115. Tests [[04 - Process of Labor and Birth]].
stem: The active management of the third stage of labour includes:

options.html: Oxytocin infusion, cord traction, fundal massage
Maternal surveillance for complications related to autotransfusion
Assessment of cervical length and administration of progesterone
Insertion of an intrauterine pressure catheter

answer:
The correct answer is A. The third stage runs from delivery of the fetus to expulsion of the placenta. Per WHO guidelines, active management of placental delivery includes:

  • Uterotonic agents (oxytocin/ergot)
  • Gentle traction of the umbilical cord
  • Fundal massage, to prevent inversion of the uterus

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Contraindications to labour and vaginal delivery include:
answer: The correct answer is E. All four are contraindications to labour and vaginal delivery: placenta previa, abnormal fetal lie, active genital herpes, and a prior classical caesarean (a vertical uterine incision, which carries a far higher rupture risk than the usual low transverse incision).

flags.title: Workbook error — the explanation belongs to a different question
flags.html:
The key reads in full: "88. Answer: E and 40% fetal). 16.7 lb. should go to the maternal component of the weight gain->to uterus, breasts, blood, water, fat. The other 10.6lb goes to fetal component->fetus, placenta, amniotic fluid."

That is a stray fragment about the distribution of pregnancy weight gain (~60% maternal / 40% fetal), which has nothing to do with contraindications to vaginal delivery. The letter E is correct; the explanation above is reconstructed. The orphaned fact is still worth knowing: of ~27 lb total gain, 16.7 lb is maternal (uterus, breasts, blood, water, fat) and 10.6 lb is fetal (fetus, placenta, amniotic fluid).

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Management of macrosomia in pregnancy should include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.html: Induction of labour at term with favourable cervix

answer:
The correct answer is C. Umbilical artery Doppler is an important tool for assessing growth restriction — but it is not needed in macrosomia, because placental insufficiency is not the concern here. This is the mirror image of Q98.

Management of macrosomia: rule out causes including gestational diabetes, review nutrition and exercise to manage weight gain, U/S assessment of weight, and possible induction at term if the cervix is favourable. It may also include caesarean section for fetal weight >5 kg, or >4.5 kg in diabetic mothers.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman at term presents in active labor with cervical dilation of 8 cm. The fetal heart rate tracing shows a Category II pattern. Which of the following is an appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Continue labor and re-evaluate the fetal heart rate tracing in 30 minutes
Administer a bolus of crystalloid fluid and position the patient in the left lateral decubitus position
Attempt operative vaginal delivery with forceps or vacuum extraction

answer:
The correct answer is A. Fetal heart rate tracings are categorized I, II or III. A Category II pattern is indeterminate and requires further evaluation and consideration of interventions — not immediate action.

The appropriate next step is to continue labour and re-evaluate the tracing in 30 minutes, which allows time for the fetus to recover from transient hypoxic episodes and for labour to progress. If the tracing remains Category II or worsens to Category III, further interventions — amnioinfusion, fetal scalp sampling, or expedited delivery — may become necessary.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q88, Q99, Q123, Q137. Tests [[05 - Abnormal Labor]].
stem: Which of the following scenarios are NOT an indication for a C-section?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The full list of indications for a C/S: abnormal FHR, fetal malpresentation (e.g. breech), dystocia, maternal HSV/HIV infection, fetal congenital abnormalities, abnormal placentation (e.g. abruption), masses, multiple gestation, cervical cancer.

Maternal diabetes is not itself an indication — though note from Q99 that a diabetic mother with an estimated fetal weight >4.5 kg may need one for macrosomia.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q107. Tests [[06 - Hemorrhagic Schock]].
stem: Which of the following is/are true regarding post-partum hemorrhage?

options.html: >500 ml blood loss for C-section or >1000 ml for vaginal delivery
Most common cause of maternal mortality worldwide
Sheehan's syndrome is a potential complication
Oxytocin is used for prevention of PPH only

answer:
The correct answer is G (B and C). Both distractor statements are true-sounding but have a detail flipped:

  • A has the thresholds swapped. PPH is >1000 mL for C-section or >500 mL for vaginal delivery — or loss of any volume that causes hemodynamic instability.
  • D is wrong because of the word "only". Oxytocin is used for prevention of PPH and as a uterotonic agent to treat an atonic uterus during active hemorrhage.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: Which of the following statements is true of "post-partum blues"?

options.html: Mood changes associated with post-partum blues are generally self-limited.
The most common time to experience post-partum blues is approximately 2-4 weeks following delivery.
Symptoms of post-partum blues often include extreme disinterest in the baby and suicidal or homicidal ideation.

answer:
The correct answer is A. Every wrong option is a postpartum depression fact mislabelled as blues — that is the entire question:

Post-partum bluesPost-partum depression
Frequency~85% of women (so C's 15% is wrong)10-20%
Onsetday 3-10 (so B's 2-4 weeks is wrong)within 6 months of delivery
Courseself-limited, lasts ~2 weeksas for depression
Severe features—disinterest in the baby, homicidal or suicidal ideation (so D is wrong)
Treatment—antidepressants + counselling/therapy

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your office 6 weeks post partum, after giving birth to a healthy baby boy. She has been doing generally well but has noticed that recently she is experiencing pain in her nipples during breastfeeding, and that her nipples appear to be cracked and dry. She has continued with breastfeeding despite this change. Her infant son has been doing well, although she does state that he appears to have patchy white spots on the inside of his mouth. What is the most appropriate management of this patient's problem?

options.html: Topical nystatin to the nipple and infant's mouth
Continue breastfeeding, heat application to breast, fluids, rest

answer:
The correct answer is B. The white patches in the infant's mouth, plus cracked nipples and pain with feeding, make this a candidal infection. Management is topical nystatin cream to the infant's mouth and the areola after each feed for 2 weeks, then qhs for another 2 weeks.

E is the near-miss: oral fluconazole is another option but is not the most appropriate, because it is associated with serious side effects. A treats breast engorgement. C (plus antibiotics) is the treatment for mastitis.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Workbook Q116, Q120, Q125. Tests [[08 - Postpartum Care]].
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 4 days after a vaginal delivery with complaints of heavy vaginal bleeding. She has been passing clots and soaking through 2 pads per hour for the past 12 hours. She denies fever, chills, or abdominal pain. On physical exam, the uterus is tender and enlarged to the level of the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D — but the workbook contradicts itself here.

The misplaced explanation is still worth keeping for its own content: PPH is >500 mL after vaginal delivery or >1000 mL after caesarean (compare Q107). The most common cause of PPH is uterine atony — a soft, boggy, poorly contracted uterus that fails to achieve hemostasis at the placental attachment site. Risk factors for atony: prolonged labour, multiple gestation, macrosomia, chorioamnionitis. Retained placenta or membranes can also cause PPH but is less likely given the 4-day timing and absence of fever.

flags.title: Workbook error — the key's explanations are off by one from Q125 onward
flags.html:
The key states only "125. Answer: D" (endometritis) with no explanation. It then attaches to Q126 an explanation that reads "126. Answer: B. Uterine atony. Postpartum hemorrhage is defined as blood loss of greater than 500 mL after vaginal delivery... In the scenario described, the patient presents with heavy vaginal bleeding, clots, and uterine tenderness and enlargement, which are all consistent with uterine atony."

That explanation is unmistakably about this question, not Q126 (which asks about fetal energy sources) — and it argues for B, uterine atony, directly contradicting the letter D printed against Q125. The drift continues: Q144's explanation is the answer to Q126. So from here the key's letters stay aligned but its prose runs one question behind.

Which is right? The clinical details favour the printed D: PPH at 4 days is secondary PPH, and uterine tenderness is the endometritis finding. True uterine atony causes primary PPH within 24 h and gives a soft, boggy uterus — the misplaced explanation even says "soft, boggy... poorly contracted", which does not match this stem's tender, enlarged uterus. The explanation also concedes that endometritis "may cause uterine tenderness" but dismisses it for absence of fever. Treat D as the answer and B as a defensible distractor; verify against a real source.

stem: The three factors necessary for lactation are:
answer: The correct answer is D. Prolactin (anterior pituitary) and oxytocin (posterior pituitary) are the endocrine triggers necessary for milk production. Milk removal — by infant or pump — is the third factor, and must begin by day 3 after birth to drive lactogenesis forward. See 09 - Lactation.

stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to breastfeeding?

options.html: HIV infection in a developing country

answer:
The correct answer is D. Active psychosis is a contraindication to breastfeeding, because of the risk of the mother harming the baby.

A is deliberately qualified: HIV infection is a contraindication in developed countries, but not in underdeveloped countries, because there the risks of GI disease/infection from formula outweigh the risk of HIV transmission. Smoking, alcohol and SSRI use are not contraindications, although smoking is strongly discouraged.

stem: What is the significance of the first 4-6 minutes of each breastfeeding?

options.html: The first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the highest content of fat, therefore promoting infant satiety and maternal weight loss after pregnancy.
The first 4-6 minutes of each feed has the most impact on hormonal levels, leading to more effective contraception in the post-partum period.
Failure to breastfeed longer than 4-6 minutes at each feed may contribute to breast engorgement and blocked ducts.
The first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the highest amount of protein.

answer: The correct answer is D. The breast milk in the first 4-6 minutes of each feed contains the majority of the protein for that feed. After this point the milk becomes richer in fat, which promotes satiety — so A has the order exactly backwards.

stem: The primary reason that APGAR scores are recorded in newborns is

options.html: To assess the need for resuscitation
To assess the probability of perinatal morbidity
To provide a common measurement to be used in research studies

answer: The correct answer is A. APGAR scores are used primarily to assess the need for resuscitation, and to monitor the effect of resuscitative efforts over time. They are not predictive of future IQ.

stem: If present after 7 months, which of the following reflexes suggests cerebral palsy?
answer: The correct answer is B. The ATNR or "fencing" reflex is present in newborns and should be gone by 6 months of age. Its presence after 7 months is ALWAYS abnormal, and typically suggests cerebral palsy.

stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the appropriate management of a case of neonatal sepsis?
answer: The correct answer is C. Expectant management is NEVER part of the management of neonatal sepsis. The infant should be started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, which may be narrowed once blood culture results are available.

stem: What is the purpose of uterine artery remodeling during pregnancy?

options.html: To allow for detachment of the placenta after labour
To maintain an adequately high blood pressure
To lower blood pressure and allow adequate blood flow to the fetus
To increase blood flow in the mother by decreasing the oxygen demand of the placenta and fetus
To allow for regular fluctuations in blood supply to the placenta and fetus

stem: Which of the following should be used in the prevention of pre-eclampsia in low risk women?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Calcium supplementation is useful in both high- and low-risk women if dietary calcium intake is low.
